title: APRA deputy chair defends super board tenure limits
full_text:
APRA deputy chair David Bradbury has defended the regulator's proposed tenure limits for superannuation fund boards, saying good governance requires board renewal and fresh challenges.
Speaking at the Australian Council of Trade Union Superannuation Forum, Bradbury noted strong views in the room about aspects of the proposals, particularly the question of tenure limits.
The prudential regulator proposed the changes to standard CPS 510 Governance in June this year, consulting to stamp out poor practices and raise expectations for boards and senior leadership teams.
Part of the reform includes introducing a 12-year default tenure limit for non-executive directors for the boards, supported by renewal and succession planning requirements. In its consultation APRA said it is intended to achieve sustainable board renewal balancing continuity with fresh perspectives.
While most submissions to the consultation agreed with the benefits of renewal and supported the need to manage succession planning, many opposed a fixed tenure limit of 10 years, arguing boards ought to retain flexibility. Some submissions advocated for tenure limits to be in guidance, or to be set at 12 years rather than 10 years.
"Let me be clear," Bradbury said.
"APRA is not questioning the value of equal representation. Nor are we seeking to veto who sits on trustee boards.
"But we do believe good governance requires renewal, fresh challenge and the capabilities needed to help trustees confront the high-stakes and rapidly evolving risks they face in today's volatile and uncertain world."
He said APRA hoped to achieve a common ground to achieve its objective.
"While acknowledging that there will be differences on the precise mechanisms used, I hope there is common ground around the objective of ensuring that boards are well equipped to protect members' interests and steer their organisations through the challenges ahead," he said.
Bradbury added with 2.5 million more Australians to move into retirement over the next decade, trustees will need the breadth of capabilities to manage financial and non-financial risks.
"That is why building capability and strengthening governance across all APRA-regulated entities, banks, insurers and superannuation trustees, is such an important priority for us," he said.
"Governance is not an end in itself. Good governance is ultimately about ensuring that boards have the capabilities, judgement, diversity of perspective and capacity for challenge needed to navigate an increasingly demanding environment."
APRA is expected to publish the final version of the standard by end of this year.
